title: Async Basics
intro: An `async fn` returns a future: a value that describes some work and has not done it. Nothing runs until something polls the future, and `.await` is how one future waits for another. The standard library defines the `Future` trait and the types around it, and has no runtime to poll futures for you: you write a small one to see the idea, and use a crate such as Tokio for real programs.

coming_from.go: Go has no `async` and `await`, and no future value to hold. `go f()` starts `f` running alongside you, and a call that has to wait is an ordinary call. A Rust `async fn` differs on both counts: calling it builds a future that has not started, and `.await` marks each place where it waits. The scheduler that goroutines get from the language is, in Rust, a runtime that you choose.
coming_from.kotlin: A `suspend fun` is the nearest thing: it can stop and be resumed later, and a suspend call looks like a plain call where Rust marks each wait with `.await`. The program above builds a coroutine with the standard library's `createCoroutine`, which does not start it, as an async call builds a future. Everyday Kotlin uses `launch` and `async` from `kotlinx.coroutines`, a library as Rust's runtimes are; they are scheduled at once, like `tokio::spawn`, unlike a bare Rust future (shown below).
coming_from.python: `async def` and `await` work as you know them, and a coroutine object is lazy like a Rust future: calling `task()` runs nothing, as the program above shows. `asyncio.run` is the event loop that Python includes; Rust includes none, so you add a runtime. Python warns when an unawaited coroutine is collected, at run time; Rust warns at compile time, when the result of an async call is discarded.
coming_from.typescript: A promise is eager: calling an `async function` runs its body up to the first `await` before you get the promise back, as the program above prints. A Rust future is lazy: nothing runs until it is polled. Node's event loop is built in; Rust's runtime is a library you add.
coming_from.java: Java has no `async` and `await`. `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync` starts at once on a pool, and virtual threads let you write plain blocking code. A Rust future needs no thread of its own: it is a value that something polls, on whatever thread the runtime chooses. A thread that is built but not started is the nearest to "created, not running" (the program above).
coming_from.csharp: `async` and `await` come from the same idea, and a `Task` is the nearest type. A C# async method starts running before the call returns, up to its first await that has to wait, so the `Task` you get is already running, as the program above prints. A Rust future has not started. The runtime is a crate, not a part of the framework.
coming_from.c: C has no futures or `async`/`await`. A function pointer is the nearest thing in the language: holding it runs nothing until you call it. A Rust `async fn` becomes a value that remembers where it stopped, and a runtime calls `poll` on it again and again until it is ready.
coming_from.cpp: C++20 coroutines are the nearest match. The compiler does the transformation, and a promise type decides what happens at creation: the program above is lazy because `initial_suspend` returns `std::suspend_always`, as a Rust future is. Rust's standard library has the `Future` trait and `Poll`; the runtime that drives them is a crate.

notes: Calling an `async fn` does not run it. It returns a future, and the compiler warns when you ignore the result of the call (`futures do nothing unless you .await or poll them`).

A future is polled and answers `Ready(value)` or `Pending`. `.await` polls an inner future and, if it is `Pending`, makes the outer future `Pending` too. A `Waker` is how a future asks to be polled again.

The standard library has no runtime. The `block_on` on this page is about ten lines, and shows all a runtime does at its core: poll until ready. The real one, with timers, I/O and spawning tasks, is [Tokio](/build/tokio/).

A task that never awaits holds its thread until it finishes, so blocking inside async code stalls the other tasks on that thread. A future that is moved to another thread must be `Send`, which includes everything it keeps across an `.await`.

gotcha.title: Using the result of an async function as if it were the value
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, Kotlin and C, a call that waits gives you the result, so `n + 1` just works. Even where the call gives you a promise or a task, it is easy to write the call and keep going.
gotcha.rust_sees: `load_count()` is a call to an async function, and an async function returns a future, not a `u32`. The compiler says so ("calling an async function returns a future") and suggests `.await`.
gotcha.why: The type of the call is `impl Future<Output = u32>`, so putting it where a `u32` is wanted is a type error and not a silent wrong result. `.await` is only legal inside an `async` function or block, and `main` is not one, so `fixed.rs` also needs something to run the future. It uses `block_on`, ten lines of standard library code; a real program uses a runtime.

go.says: Go has no async functions. `loadCount()` is an ordinary call that returns the number, and the program prints count: 4.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints count: 4. A `suspend` call looks like a plain call and returns the `Int`, with no `await` to write.

python.says: Python raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'coroutine' and 'int'` when it reaches `n + 1`, and warns that the coroutine was never awaited. The mistake is the same; Python finds it while the program runs.

import asyncio


async def load_count():
    return 3


async def report():
    n = load_count()
    return n + 1


print("count:", asyncio.run(report()))

lazy.py.code:
import asyncio


async def fetch_name():
    print("  fetch_name body runs")
    return "ferris"


async def leaf():
    pass  # finishes at once, so awaiting it does not suspend main


async def main():
    print("calling fetch_name()")
    coroutine = fetch_name()
    print("called it:", type(coroutine).__name__, "- the body has not run")
    print("name:", await coroutine)

    # create_task hands the coroutine to the event loop, which starts it when main next suspends
    task = asyncio.create_task(fetch_name())
    print("task created; still has not run")
    await leaf()
    print("after awaiting leaf(), which never waits: done =", task.done())
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    print("after asyncio.sleep(0), which does suspend: done =", task.done())
    await task

    # a coroutine that is never awaited is reported when it is garbage collected
    fetch_name()
    print("called without await")


asyncio.run(main())
